1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: The patient is a 57-year-old man from Sichuan who first presented to our hospital in approximately 34 months before Day 0 and was admitted to the TB ward of the Department of Respiratory Medicine. Chief complaint: "Back pain for more than 7 months, intermittent cough and dyspnea for 5 months." More than 7 months before this admission, the patient developed right-sided back pain without an obvious trigger, localized to the area below the right scapula. The pain could worsen in either the left or right lateral decubitus position. There was no fever, cough, sputum production, hemoptysis, dyspnea, or other discomfort. He was seen at a local hospital, where after evaluation he was considered to have "pneumonia" and was treated with medications including "levofloxacin" for 19 days. The patient felt his symptoms were slightly relieved. Repeat chest CT at the Provincial People’s Hospital (Day -1256) showed patchy confluent opacities, linear opacities, and tree-in-bud pattern in the left upper lobe, right middle lobe, and medial basal segment of the right lower lobe; chronic infectious disease was considered more likely. The tracheobronchial tree was patent, and no enlargement of hilar or mediastinal lymph nodes was seen. After this evaluation, the patient went to the Provincial Infectious Disease Hospital for further diagnosis and treatment. That hospital considered "bilateral pulmonary TB" and empirically started anti-TB treatment with the HL2EO regimen. Five months before this admission (i.e., after more than 1 month of anti-TB treatment), the location, severity, and pattern of the back pain had not changed significantly compared with before, and he began to have intermittent cough, expectoration of a small amount of white sticky sputum, and paroxysmal dyspnea, without fever, hemoptysis, palpitations, chest pain, headache, vomiting, diarrhea, or other discomfort. On outpatient follow-up, he continued anti-TB treatment with the "HL2EO" regimen as instructed, and after 4 months it was adjusted to "HL2E" anti-TB treatment. Two months before this admission, the patient underwent repeat chest CT at the Infectious Disease Hospital (Day -1113), which showed bilateral punctate, patchy, consolidative, and linear opacities, with secondary pulmonary TB considered more likely. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy showed funnel-shaped stenosis of the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe, with moss-like necrotic material obstructing the subsegmental bronchial opening; the entire mucosa was hyperemic and rough; no obvious abnormality was seen in the left bronchus. "Bronchial TB?" was considered. The patient then presented to our hospital’s TB clinic for further diagnosis and treatment and was admitted from the outpatient clinic with "Bronchial TB?" Since illness onset, his mental status, appetite, and sleep were fairly good, bowel and bladder habits were normal, and body weight had decreased by 3 kg. He had previously been healthy, with no special past medical history, denied a history of hepatitis or TB and denied close contact history, and had no history of drug allergy. He had smoked for more than 20 years, about 4 cigarettes/day, and had quit smoking for half a year. Marital/reproductive history and family history were unremarkable. Physical examination on admission: temperature 36.6℃, heart rate 88/min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 117/73 mmHg, SPO2 99%, no enlargement of superficial lymph nodes throughout the body. Bilateral respiratory movement was normal, tactile fremitus was symmetric, percussion of both lungs was resonant, breath sounds in the right lower lung were slightly decreased, no dry or moist rales were heard, and no pleural friction rub was present. Cardiac, abdominal, and neurologic examinations showed no abnormalities. There was no edema of either lower extremity and no clubbing. Ancillary examinations: Laboratory tests: CRP 7.07 mg/L; PCT, ESR, and IL-6 were normal. Fungal G test and GM test were negative. Immune testing and tumor markers were all without abnormalities. Repeated sputum smear and culture for bacteria, fungi, and TB were all negative. TB-DNA in sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was negative, and no malignant cells were found. Imaging examinations: chest CT in approximately 36 months before Day 0 showed multiple bilateral areas of consolidation with small cavity formation; scattered patchy, linear, and small nodular opacities in both lungs; mild focal bronchiectatic change; adjacent pleural thickening and adhesion; findings were mostly infectious lesions, with other causes to be excluded; calcified foci in the right lower lobe and hilum; no obvious cardiac enlargement. ECG and echocardiography showed no abnormalities. Bronchoscopy: fiberoptic bronchoscopy showed cicatricial occlusion of the bronchial opening of the anterior basal segment of the right lower lobe with localized gray-black carbon dust deposition; swelling of the bronchial mucosa of the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe with granulomatous hyperplasia and luminal narrowing; no obvious abnormality in the left bronchus. Bronchoscopic pathology (dorsal segment of right lower lobe): severe chronic inflammation of the bronchial mucosa. Brush smear did not detect acid-fast bacilli or fungi. In around Day 0, the patient presented to our hospital for the second time. Chief complaint: "Recurrent back pain with intermittent cough and sputum production for more than 3 years, worsened for 2 weeks." Since the last discharge, anti-TB treatment had been stopped after about 1 year. He still had recurrent intermittent back pain and cough. Two weeks earlier, after catching a cold, he developed cough again, characterized as paroxysmal and worse at night, accompanied by dark yellow purulent sputum and pain in the right scapular region, without chest tightness, dyspnea, fever, etc.; he was admitted from the outpatient clinic with "Bronchiectasis with infection: old TB?; right lower lobe atelectasis." Physical examination on admission: breath sounds in the right lower lung were slightly decreased; the rest of the examination was unremarkable. Further examinations after admission: infection markers: CRP 7.07 mmg/L, ESR, PCT, and CBC were normal, fungal G and GM tests were negative; TB-IGRA (T-N) 143.23 pg/ml, sputum smear and culture were negative (no Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolated after 6 weeks of culture), sputum TB-DNA negative; immune markers: CD4 cell subset 19.2%, CD8 cell subset 48.3%, CD4/CD8 0.4, IGM 2500 mg/L, ANA suspiciously positive (±); tumor markers: CEA 4.57 ng/ml, CA19-9 220.9 U/ml, CA15-3 48.91 U/ml, CA-125 245 U/ml. ECG was normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed cholesterol deposition in the gallbladder wall. Repeat chest CT on Day 0 showed multiple bilateral areas of consolidation with small cavity formation; scattered patchy, linear, and small nodular opacities in both lungs; mild focal bronchiectatic change; adjacent pleural thickening and adhesion; findings were mostly infectious lesions, with other causes to be excluded. Calcified foci in the right lower lobe and hilum. (Bilateral lung lesions were somewhat larger than in 2014.) Fiberoptic bronchoscopy: stenosis of the bronchi of the dorsal and basal segments of the right lower lobe. BALF smear and culture, TB-DNA, and exfoliated cells were negative. In approximately 26 months after Day 0, the patient presented to our hospital for the third time. Chief complaint: "Recurrent back pain with cough and sputum production for more than 5 years, worsened with fever for half a month." Half a month earlier, without an obvious trigger, the patient’s cough, sputum production, and other symptoms worsened compared with before, accompanied by fever with a maximum temperature of 38.9℃, yellow purulent sputum, blood-streaked sputum, and night sweats, without chills, chest tightness, palpitations, edema of both lower extremities, etc. He was seen at a local county people’s hospital, where chest CT showed extensive consolidation in the apicoposterior segment and dorsal segment of the left upper lobe and the dorsal segment of the right upper lobe and lower lobe, with bronchial shadows and calcific shadows visible within; inflammatory change in the anterior segment of the left upper lobe. He was treated with ambroxol for expectoration, levofloxacin, and cefoperazone for anti-infective therapy, but there was no obvious improvement, so he was transferred to our hospital for further diagnosis and treatment. Since the onset of this episode, his diet and sleep were acceptable, bowel and bladder habits were normal, and there had been no obvious change in body weight. Physical examination on admission: vital signs were normal, breath sounds in the right lower lung were decreased, the remaining lung breath sounds were clear, no dry or moist rales or pleural friction rub were heard, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Chest CT in approximately 36 months before Day 0 showed multiple areas of consolidation in both lungs, with small cavity formation; scattered patchy, linear, and small nodular opacities in both lungs; mild focal bronchiectasis; and adjacent pleural thickening and adhesion, mostly consistent with infectious lesions.

Fiberoptic bronchoscopy showed funnel-shaped stenosis of the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe; moss-like necrotic material obstructing the subsegmental opening; diffuse mucosal hyperemia and roughness throughout. Bronchial TB? had previously been considered clinically.

The patient has intermittent cough, expectoration of a small amount of white mucoid sputum, paroxysmal dyspnea, and weight loss of 3 kg, consistent with manifestations of chronic pulmonary infectious disease.

differential_diagnoses.name: Nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease (with possible endobronchial involvement)
supporting_evidence: Chest CT shows a tree-in-bud pattern, small nodules, areas of consolidation, small cavities, and mild focal bronchiectasis, which are imaging findings seen in chronic mycobacterial infection
Prolonged disease course, multifocal involvement of both lungs, with only slight improvement after conventional antibacterial therapy

Multiple sputum smears and cultures for TB were negative, and TB-DNA was negative, but imaging and bronchoscopy still suggested chronic infectious lesions; nontuberculous mycobacterial infection should be considered.

Bronchoscopy showed swelling of the bronchial mucosa in the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe, with granulation-like proliferation and luminal narrowing, suggesting possible chronic granulomatous airway disease.
opposing_evidence: Phase 1 data did not provide positive culture or molecular evidence for nontuberculous mycobacteria
On Day -1113, follow-up CT imaging was interpreted as most likely secondary pulmonary tuberculosis.
The phase 1 information did not provide clear contradictory evidence.

differential_diagnoses.name: Central lung cancer or lung cancer with obstructive pneumonia/post-obstructive changes
supporting_evidence: The patient is a 57-year-old man with a smoking history of more than 20 years.
Chief complaint of chronic right-sided back pain, followed by cough and dyspnea, with the possibility of an intrathoracic mass or obstructive lesion

Bronchoscopy showed infundibular stenosis of the dorsal segmental bronchus of the right lower lobe, with the subsegmental opening obstructed by necrotic material; subsequent bronchoscopy later the same year showed scar-related occlusion of the bronchial opening of the anterior basal segment of the right lower lobe, and mucosal swelling with granulation-like proliferation and luminal narrowing of the dorsal segmental bronchus of the right lower lobe, suggesting a focal obstructive bronchial lesion and the need for vigilance for tumor.

Chest CT showed multiple areas of consolidation in both lungs with small cavity formation, mild focal bronchiectasis, and slightly decreased breath sounds in the right lower lung, which may be seen in post-obstructive infection/atelectasis
opposing_evidence: No enlargement of the hilar or mediastinal lymph nodes
No malignant cells were detected in sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage fluid.
Bronchoscopic biopsy (posterior segment of the right lower lobe) showed only severe chronic inflammation of the bronchial mucosa
Imaging shows multiple lesions in both lungs, which is not entirely consistent with the typical solitary mass pattern of primary lung cancer.

differential_diagnoses.name: Chronic necrotizing bacterial lung infection / lung abscess-like lesion (including recurrent post-obstructive infection)
supporting_evidence: Chest CT showed multiple areas of consolidation in both lungs, with small cavity formation, suggesting possible necrotizing pulmonary parenchymal infection

In the later stage, the patient developed intermittent cough, expectoration of a small amount of white mucoid sputum, and paroxysmal dyspnea, consistent with manifestations of chronic airway-parenchymal lung infection.
Bronchoscopy showed necrotic material causing obstruction, mucosal hyperemia and roughness, and granulation-like proliferation, which may be associated with chronic pyogenic infection.
Breath sounds in the right lower lung are slightly decreased, suggesting persistent localized pulmonary pathology
opposing_evidence: The onset and course of the disease were relatively slow, with no obvious systemic infectious toxic manifestations such as fever or chills.
CRP was only 7.07 mg/L; PCT, ESR, and IL-6 were normal, which does not support active severe bacterial infection.
Multiple sputum smears and bacterial cultures were all negative
After 19 days of levofloxacin treatment, only slight subjective symptom relief was reported, with no clear imaging evidence of improvement.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary fungal infection (chronic pulmonary aspergillosis, etc.)
supporting_evidence: Chest CT shows multiple areas of consolidation, small cavity formation, and a chronic protracted course; these are findings that can be seen in some chronic pulmonary fungal infections.
Bronchoscopy previously showed lichen-like necrotic material causing obstruction and granulomatous-like proliferative lesions, which require differentiation from fungal airway disease
After conventional antibacterial treatment and empiric anti-TB treatment, the clinical problem persists; infection with atypical pathogens should be considered.
opposing_evidence: Fungal G test and GM test negative
Multiple sputum smears and cultures for fungi were negative
No fungi detected on smear
The patient was previously in good health, and the information from the first stage did not indicate a definite immunosuppressed background.

differential_diagnoses.name: Organizing pneumonia/chronic inflammatory granulomatous disease (e.g., cryptogenic organizing pneumonia or other noninfectious inflammation)
supporting_evidence: Chest CT showed multiple areas of consolidation, patchy opacities, and linear opacities in both lungs, which are among the imaging patterns seen in organizing inflammation.

Repeated infectious disease workup was negative, including sputum smear and culture, TB-DNA, and fungus-related tests, suggesting that atypical infection or noninfectious inflammation should be included in the differential diagnosis.
Bronchoscopic biopsy showed only severe chronic inflammation of the bronchial mucosa, with no direct evidence of TB, fungal infection, or malignancy obtained.
opposing_evidence: The presence of a tree-in-bud pattern, small cavitary formation, and intrabronchial obstruction by necrotic material is more suggestive of an infectious or obstructive lesion.
Focal bronchial stenosis and cicatricial occlusion are not typical manifestations of simple organizing pneumonia
The phase 1 information did not provide clear contradictory evidence.

stage2_input.text: Laboratory tests: ESR 29 mm/h; CBC, CRP, PCT, creatinine and renal function, fungal G test, and GM test were normal; Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydia antibodies, cryptococcal antigen, 13 respiratory viruses, TORCH, and multiple sputum smear and culture results were all negative. EB-DNA 1.06E+02 copies/ml, CMV-DNA 8.86E+01 copies/ml, TB-IGRA (T-N) 274.19 pg/ml. Tumor marker: CEA 4.46 ng/ml. Chest CT in approximately 26 months after Day 0 showed multiple areas of consolidation in both lungs with cavitation, more prominent in the right lung; scattered small nodules and patchy/linear opacities in both lungs; mild focal bronchiectatic dilatation; adjacent pleural thickening and adhesions; on contrast-enhanced scan, no obvious vascular stenosis was seen within the areas of consolidation, mostly consistent with infectious lesions, with other etiologies to be excluded; calcified foci in the right lower lobe and hilar region; increased mediastinal and right hilar lymph nodes, some enlarged; no cardiac enlargement. (Compared with 2017, the bilateral pulmonary lesions had further increased in size.) Bronchoscopy: narrowing of the bronchial lumen in the dorsal and basal segments of the right lower lobe. BALF submitted for testing: GM, TB-DNA, TB X-pert, Pneumocystis nucleic acid, smear + culture, and cryptococcal antigen were negative.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: On Day +817, the patient underwent percutaneous lung biopsy.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient's disease course has lasted for more than 5 years, with recurrent back pain, cough, and sputum production. In 2019, fever, purulent sputum, blood-streaked sputum, and night sweats also developed. Chest CT showed multiple areas of consolidation with cavitation in both lungs; the lesions had continued to enlarge compared with 2014 and 2017, and there was long-standing stenosis of the right lower lobe bronchus. Previously, multiple sputum and BALF bacterial/fungal/mycobacterial tests, as well as TB-DNA and X-pert, were all negative. Neither conventional anti-infective therapy nor a prolonged course of anti-TB treatment showed definite efficacy. Bronchoscopic biopsy showed only chronic inflammation and still could not explain the progressive lesions. At this point, direct acquisition of tissue from the pulmonary parenchymal lesions was needed to address the key question of whether this represented infection, pneumonic-type lung cancer, lymphoma, or another chronic inflammatory/lymphoproliferative disease. Percutaneous lung biopsy can obtain relatively representative tissue from imaging-visible lesions, providing the basis for subsequent pathology, immunohistochemistry, and molecular testing, and was the core tissue-sampling procedure for establishing the diagnosis and guiding subsequent treatment decisions in this case.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Postoperative pathology: Microscopic examination showed marked infiltration of small cells and a lymphoproliferative lesion; the proliferating cells were predominantly small lymphocytes.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: After obtaining lung tissue, the nature of the lesion must first be assessed through routine histopathologic morphology. This patient had long undergone repeated differential consideration among multiple diagnoses, including TB, chronic infection, and pneumonic-type lung cancer, but microbiologic studies remained consistently negative and imaging showed continuous progression, indicating that imaging and clinical manifestations alone were insufficient to characterize the lesion. Postoperative pathology can directly evaluate the cellular components within the lesion, their distribution pattern, and whether necrosis, granulomas, epithelial tumor, or abnormal lymphoid cell infiltration is present, thereby determining whether the lesion is more consistent with infectious inflammation, an epithelial malignancy, or a lymphoproliferative disorder. In this case, microscopy showed prominent small-cell infiltration and a lymphoproliferative lesion composed predominantly of small lymphocytes, clearly shifting the diagnostic direction from the long-suspected infection toward lymphoma-related disease and providing a basis for further immunophenotyping and clonality testing.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Immunohistochemistry showed: tumor cells CD20 (+), CD79a (+), CD3 (-), CD5 (-), CD23 (-), CD10 (-), Cyclin D1 (-), CD43 (+), CD30 (-), TdT (-), IgG4 (-), bcl-6 (weakly +), SOX-11 (-), CD21 and CD23 showed an incomplete follicular dendritic cell network, Ki-67 (+, 3%-5%).
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Morphologic findings of small lymphocytic infiltration alone cannot distinguish reactive lymphoid hyperplasia from true lymphoma, nor can they define the specific subtype. In this patient, with long-term progression of multiple pulmonary consolidations, lesions distributed in both lungs, insufficient routine systemic evidence of infection, and pathology suggesting lymphoid proliferation, immunohistochemistry is essential to determine cell lineage and classification. CD20 and CD79a positivity indicate B-cell lineage, and CD3 negativity excludes a T-cell lesion; combinations of CD5, CD10, CD23, CyclinD1, and SOX-11 help exclude other small B-cell lymphomas such as CLL/SLL, follicular lymphoma, and mantle cell lymphoma; a low Ki-67 proliferative index also supports features of an indolent lymphoma. The clinical significance of this test is to confirm that the lesion is not simply chronic inflammation, nor common lung cancer, but rather an indolent B-cell lymphoproliferative lesion, and to further support the final diagnosis of pulmonary MALT lymphoma, thereby directly affecting subsequent referral to hematology and selection of a chemotherapy regimen.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Gene rearrangement testing: a clonal IgH amplification peak was detected.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Lung tissue pathology and immunohistochemistry have already suggested B-cell lymphoproliferation, but reactive lymphocytosis may also occur in the setting of chronic pulmonary inflammation, so molecular biologic methods are still needed to determine whether clonality is present. This patient had an especially long disease course, and the imaging findings of multiple areas of consolidation were extremely similar to infection; previously, the patient had also been treated long-term as TB and infection, so any diagnostic revision must be supported by stronger evidence. IgH gene rearrangement testing can determine whether the B cells represent clonal expansion and is an important adjunct for distinguishing reactive lymphoid hyperplasia from B-cell lymphoma. Detection of an IgH clonal expansion peak indicates monoclonal B-cell proliferation, further supporting the diagnosis of malignant lymphoma, reducing the risk of misclassifying it as chronic inflammation or pseudolymphoma, and increasing the reliability of the final pathologic classification.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Further PET-CT: multiple consolidations and patchy opacities in the left upper lobe and right lung, more prominent in the right lower lobe; the lesions are irregular in morphology, with mild corresponding bronchial dilatation. The bilateral pulmonary consolidations show varying degrees of increased 18F-FDG uptake, most prominent in the right lower lobe lesion; no other abnormally increased 18F-FDG uptake is seen elsewhere in the body.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: After pathology had already suggested lymphoma, it was still necessary to define the extent of the lesions, metabolic activity, and whether there was extrapulmonary involvement, in order to determine whether this was primary pulmonary lymphoma or systemic lymphoma involving the lungs, and to provide a basis for staging and treatment planning. In this patient, imaging had long shown multiple consolidations, patchy opacities, and mild bronchiectasis in both lungs, which could easily be confused with infection or pneumonic-type lung cancer; meanwhile, the 2019 CT showed increased mediastinal and right hilar lymph nodes, some of which were enlarged, also requiring evaluation of their systemic distribution. PET-CT can assess 18F-FDG uptake at the whole-body level, helping both to confirm the extent of active intrapulmonary lesions and to select representative lesions, and also to screen for extrapulmonary lymph node involvement or involvement of other organs. The results showed increased metabolic activity in the bilateral pulmonary lesions, while no abnormal hypermetabolic uptake was seen elsewhere in the body, supporting that the disease was mainly confined to the lungs, consistent with the clinical features of primary pulmonary MALT lymphoma, and providing a baseline for subsequent referral to the hematology department for treatment and for treatment response follow-up.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: On Day +817, the patient underwent a percutaneous lung biopsy. Postoperative pathology: Microscopy showed extensive small-cell infiltration and a lymphoproliferative lesion; the proliferating cells were predominantly small lymphocytes. Immunohistochemistry showed: tumor cells CD20 (+), CD79a (+), CD3 (-), CD5 (-), CD23 (-), CD10 (-), CyclinD1 (-), CD43 (+), CD30 (-), TdT (-), IgG4 (-), bcl-6 (weak +), SOX-11 (-), CD21 and CD23 showed an incomplete follicular dendritic cell network, Ki-67 (+, 3%-5%). Gene rearrangement testing: clonal amplification peak of IgH detected. Further PET-CT showed multiple areas of consolidation and patchy opacities in the left upper lobe and right lung, more prominent in the right lower lobe; the lesions were irregular in morphology, with mild corresponding bronchial dilatation; the bilateral pulmonary consolidations showed varying degrees of increased 18F-FDG uptake, most prominent in the right lower lobe lesion; no abnormally increased 18F-FDG uptake was seen elsewhere in the body.

8.final_diagnosis_and_diagnostic_basis.final_diagnosis: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue of the lung.
diagnostic_basis: Based on the morphologic and immunohistochemical findings, the pathologic diagnosis is non-Hodgkin lymphoma, an indolent B-cell lymphoma, consistent with extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (WHO, MALT).

treatment_plan: After transfer to the Department of Hematology for further treatment, the patient subsequently underwent 9 cycles of chemotherapy from approximately 28 months after Day 0 to approximately 47 months after Day 0.
treatment_response: Repeat PET-CT showed a decrease in the size of the left upper lobe lesion, decreased glucose metabolism in the right lung lesion compared with before, and no abnormally increased 18F-FDG uptake in the remaining parts of the body.
